blocks.text: **Glenohumeral osteoarthritis (GH OA)** is a degenerative condition of the ball-and-socket shoulder joint in which the joint cartilage thins and the bone changes, with pain and stiffness. It is less common than knee or hip OA and is more often seen in older adults, after past shoulder injury or dislocation, after some surgeries, or with long-standing rotator cuff problems [Ref - to verify].

OA is a whole-joint condition, not simply wear and tear. The relationship between X-ray changes and pain is imperfect, so treatment is guided by symptoms and function, not images alone [Ref - to verify].

items: Deep, aching shoulder pain, often poorly localised, worse with use and at night.
Gradual stiffness, with loss of **passive** external rotation especially.
Grinding or catching with movement (crepitus).
Difficulty with dressing, reaching behind, overhead tasks and carrying.
Usually older than 50 to 60 or a history of earlier shoulder injury.

blocks.text: GH OA can look like frozen shoulder because both limit passive external rotation. The key difference is the **X-ray**, which shows joint space loss and osteophytes in OA but is usually normal in frozen shoulder.

rows: How long has the pain lasted, and is it slowly worsening?
OA is gradual; frozen shoulder moves in phases
Any past dislocation, fracture, surgery or rotator cuff tear?
Night pain, and can you lie on that side?
Other joint pain, inflammatory arthritis, steroid use, sickle cell disease?
Any fever, weight loss, constant pain?
What can you no longer do?

items: Observation of muscle wasting, swelling and posture.
Active and passive range, particularly passive external rotation at the side.
Crepitus during passive movement (feel with a hand over the joint).
Resisted tests for the cuff and biceps.
Cervical and neurological screen.
Functional tasks: hand to head, hand behind back, overhead reach.

blocks.text: Honest note: there is no accurate clinical special test for GH OA. The diagnosis is made from history, loss of passive movement, and X-ray.
E1. Passive external rotation at the side

Procedure as in Vol 5 Ch 2. **Positive:** clearly reduced passive external rotation with a hard or bony end-feel, sometimes with crepitus. Both OA and frozen shoulder can be positive, so the X-ray separates them.

rows: Place a hand over the front or back of the joint and move the arm passively through rotation or elevation
Palpable grinding or crepitus with familiar pain
Joint surface involvement, not a specific diagnosis

blocks.text: Older age, gradual pain, reduced passive external rotation and crepitus together raise the likelihood of GH OA. X-ray is requested by the doctor for confirmation [Ref - to verify].

rows: Normal X-ray, phased painful stiff course
Long-standing large cuff tear, high-riding humeral head on X-ray
Steroid use, alcohol, sickle cell disease, severe pain
Pain on top of the shoulder

sections.title: G. RED FLAGS AND URGENT CONDITIONS

rows: Sudden severe pain after minimal trauma in an older or steroid-treated patient
Rapid deterioration over weeks, severe night pain
Weight loss, cancer history, constant pain
Multiple swollen painful joints with morning stiffness

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Any emergency or urgent flag? **Yes:** act as in Section G.
Older age or past injury, gradual pain, reduced passive external rotation with crepitus? **Yes:** working diagnosis is probable GH OA; ask for an X-ray to confirm and separate from frozen shoulder.
Mild to moderate symptoms? **Yes:** start conservative care.
Severe pain, major loss of function, or no improvement after reasonable non-surgical care? **Yes:** discuss specialist review, injection or joint replacement [Ref - to verify].

rows: Supine, gentle oscillations in pain-free range

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** education and exercise. Manual therapy is optional for short-term comfort. Do not claim that mobilization rebuilds cartilage or reverses the arthritis. Avoid forceful end-range stretching because it can increase pain [Ref - to verify].

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

rows: Table slide, wall walk, stick-assisted raise
Lying, push the hand outward with the other arm

blocks.text: Exercise has not been shown to reverse the joint changes, but it may improve pain and function [Ref - to verify]. Pain up to about 3 to 4 out of 10 that settles within a day is a common guide. Weight management and general health advice may help, especially when there are other joints involved.

**Medical options:** pain medication, intra-articular corticosteroid injection (short-term relief for some), and joint replacement (anatomic or reverse, depending on the cuff and bone) for severe, persistent cases [Ref - to verify]. These are doctor decisions. Rehabilitation after surgery follows the surgeon's protocol.

items: **Visit 1:** screen flags, examine, request or review imaging through a doctor, explain OA in plain terms.
**Early:** reduce painful loading, gentle movement, optional low-grade mobilization.
**Middle:** strengthen the cuff and scapular muscles, build function and fitness.
**Late:** self-management plan for flares, activity pacing, adaptive tools.
**If no improvement:** specialist review for injection or surgical options.

blocks.text: Track pain, night pain, passive external rotation, functional tasks, strength and an outcome measure such as SPADI or the Oxford Shoulder Score [Ref - to verify].

rows: Pain and function worse despite good care

blocks.text: **Case:** A 66-year-old retired builder has 2 years of slowly worsening right shoulder pain and stiffness, with grinding when he lifts the arm. He had a dislocation 20 years ago. Passive external rotation is greatly reduced with crepitus. X-ray shows joint space narrowing and osteophytes.

**Working diagnosis:** glenohumeral osteoarthritis, probably secondary to previous dislocation. **Plan:** education, gentle range work, cuff and scapular strengthening, pain advice, review for injection or surgical discussion if function remains poor.

items: How do you separate GH OA from frozen shoulder? Both limit passive external rotation. X-ray shows joint changes in OA and is usually normal in frozen shoulder, and the clinical course differs.
Why not promise that exercise will rebuild the joint? There is no evidence that it reverses the joint changes. The aim is better pain, function and confidence.
Why is a severe sudden pain in a steroid-treated patient urgent? It may be a fracture or avascular necrosis and needs imaging.
The patient fears the X-ray means surgery. What do you say? Many people with X-ray changes manage with non-surgical care, and surgery is considered when symptoms are severe and persistent.
Why check passive range, not only active? It shows whether the limit comes from the joint itself.
**Initial approach:** education, activity modification and graded exercise.
**Justifying findings:** gradual pain, loss of passive external rotation, crepitus, X-ray changes, no flags.
**Priority:** function and pain control.
**Manual therapy:** optional gentle adjunct.
**Exercise:** range maintenance, cuff and scapular strengthening, general fitness.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** OA is common; many people do well without surgery; report fever or sudden severe pain.
**Avoid:** forceful stretching, promises of reversal.
**Measure:** pain, range, SPADI or Oxford Shoulder Score.
**If no improvement:** specialist referral.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** self-management plan established.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** adult, no infection, no fracture, mild to moderate symptoms.

items: **Can be tested:** whether exercise and education improve pain and function; outcomes of replacement compared with non-surgical care.
**Hypotheses:** that muscle strengthening reduces joint load.
**Future questions:** best exercise approach and timing of surgery.

blocks.text: Evidence not graded until references are verified.
